Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
Each of the four वेदस्, the basic scriptures of the Hindus, is divided broadly into two sections: the मन्त्र and the ब्राह्मण. The मन्त्र section contains prayers and hymns. The ब्राह्मण section deals with the application of these mantras in rituals.
The Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa forms the sixth (and the last) chapter of a bigger work called Ṣaḍviṁśa Brāhmaṇa which itself is the second of the nine ब्राह्मणस् of the Sāmaveda, available to us now. Though the first five chapters of the Ṣaḍviṁśa Brāhmaṇa deal with the ceremonies and rituals connected with the Somayāgas, the sixth one makes a comp-lete departure and deals with strange phenomena like ill-omens and the expiatory rites that help offset their effects. It is perhaps due to this reason that this particular section is thus designated (adbhuta wonderful, strange).
There are indications to prove that the Ṣaḍviṁśa Brāhmaṇa originally consisted of only five chapters and the sixth i.e., the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa was appended to it later.
The entire book deals with adbhuta-शान्तिस् or appeasement of portents, and is divided into twelve khaṇḍas or sections. The various portents indicating imminent dangers are described as being connected with the gods like इन्द्र, यम, वरुण and विष्णु; and appropriate शान्तिस् (rites of appeasement of the deities) are also given. The idea seems to be that when these gods are displeased, troubles start and when appeased through appropriate rites, they cease.
The list of portents given is quite long but interesting. Starting from the breaking or damage of household articles for apparently no reason, right up to natural calamities like earthquakes, destruction of crops and the fall of meteors, the list mentions the happening of many unnatural and improbable phenomena also. Among such, it is curious to note that temples shake and the इदोल्स् of gods laugh, weep, sing, dance or close their eyes! This is a clear indication that temples with इदोल्स् installed, had already come into being by the time of this ब्राह्मण.
The śānti rites are usually sacrificial oblations with suitable mantras addressed to the deity that has been displeased.
See also ṢAḌVIṀŚA BRĀHMAṆA.

Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
One of the two great epics of India, the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, has been the basic text for the story of राम. It has been the primary source of inspiration over the millennia, for many a poet who has retold the story in his own way, often adopting it to the philosophy of his life. One such work is the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa (‘the Wonder that is रामायण’). Though attributed to वाल्मीकि, it is obviously a late work. Scholars are divided about its being earlier or later to another, more well-known work, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (A.

). The glorification of Kālī and identifying her with सीता induce us to think that the work must have been written at a time when reconciling the राम cult of the Vaiṣṇavas and the शाक्त cults had become a social necessity. Also, the words in the colophon as seen from a printed text—‘iti ārṣe śrīmad-rāmāyaṇe vālmīkīye ādikāvye adbhutottarakāṇḍe...’—give rise to the suspicion that the writer might have attemp-ted to pass it off as an appendix to the Uttarakāṇḍa of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa.
The Adbhuta Ramayaṇa is a compa-ratively smaller work of 1355 verses spread over 27 sargas or chapters. Unlike the other Rāmāyaṇas it is not divided into kāṇḍas or books.
The contents of the work may be summarized briefly as follows: The sage Bhāradvāja approaches the great sage वाल्मीकि and requests him to give the secret teaching that is hidden in his original Rāmāyaṇa which is rather voluminous. वाल्मीकि replies that the real secret is that राम is the Highest ब्रह्मन् and सीता, the Highest प्रकृति, the power of ब्रह्मन्. Then he goes on to narrate the reasons for the descent of राम (sargas 2 to 4) and सीता (s. 5 to 7), which were apparently due to the curses of the sages नारद and Parvata, but really to destroy the wicked and protect the good. This is followed by the story of the birth of सीता as the daughter of रावण, but abandoned by his wife मण्डोदरी, and found by जनक, the king of मिथिला, in his field. After this, the events move at a terrific speed: राम’s मर्रिअगे, परशुराम’s humiliation at the hands of राम (s. 9), राम’s entering the forest along with सीता and लक्ष्मण (The entire episode of the Ayodhyākāṇḍa of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa leading to राम’s banishment is glossed over here!), सीता’s abduction by रावण and राम striking friendship with सुग्रीव and हनुमान् (s.10). In answer to the simple question that हनुमान् asks, ‘Who are you?’ (s.10) राम waxes eloquently to describe himself as the आत्मन्, परमेश्वर, Māyāvī and अन्तर्यामिन् (s. 11 and 12). Most of the ideas and even the words are reminiscent of the Bhagavadgītā, and some of the उपनिषद्स्. This is followed by a short discourse on भक्ति or devotion (s. 13) and a curious mixture of a variety of philosophical and mythological topics (s. 14). The next chapter contains a beautiful hymn of हनुमान् on राम (s. 15). The sixteenth sarga disposes off very briefly (in 20 verses) the entire story of the Yuddhakāṇḍa. In the seventeenth, सीता reveals the existence of a thousand-headed रावण, the elder brother of the ten-headed demon, and describes him as she had heard from a ब्राह्मण in her younger days. Hearing this, राम starts on an invasion of the पुष्कर द्वीप, the abode of the thousand-headed monster, in order to destroy him. In the terrific war that ensues, राम falls down unconscious (s. 18 to 22). Seeing this tragedy that had overtaken राम and his forces, सीता assumes the terrible form of Kālī and destroys the demon along with all his forces. She is helped in this by her innumerable emanations (s. 23). राम wakes up and is surprised to see Kālī there (s. 24). He praises her with a long hymn containing 1008 names (s. 25). Though called Sītā-sahasranāma (‘thousand names of सीता’) almost all the names belong to the शक्ति cult. सीता dissolves the form of Kālī and reappears in her original form. After thus gaining victory, राम returns to अयोध्या and resumes his rule (s. 26 and 27).
Though this work might have served a specific purpose during the days of its composition and later, it fails to come up to the level of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and the Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa.
See also ADHYĀTMA RĀMĀYAṆA, ĀNANDA RĀMĀYAṆA and RĀMĀYAṆA.
